stem: A CI system programmatically starts a Claude Code session for a scheduled nightly job and needs to reference that exact same session again the next night to continue a multi-night audit, without any interactive picker and without depending on it being "the most recent" session (other unrelated jobs may run in between). Which flag combination fits, and why do the two more common flags fall short here?
explanation: `--session-id <UUID>` fits, since the pipeline can generate and store the UUID itself, then reliably reattach to that exact session on any later night regardless of what else ran in between. `--continue` would fail because other jobs running between nights breaks the "most recent" assumption, and `--resume` requires an interactive picker unsuitable for an unattended job.

choices.text: --session-id <UUID> — a pipeline-controlled, stable identifier that works regardless of other jobs running in between, unlike --continue (breaks if another job ran more recently) or --resume (needs an interactive picker)
choices.reasoning: Correct: this matches the documented use case and correctly identifies why the two more common flags fall short — --continue depends on recency, which other interleaved jobs would break, and --resume requires interactivity unsuitable for an unattended nightly job.

choices.text: --continue, since it always resumes the correct session regardless of what else has run in between
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: --continue resumes the most recent session — if any other job runs in between nights, --continue would attach to that unrelated session instead of the intended audit session.

choices.text: --resume, since it lets the pipeline pick the exact session by name each night
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: --resume opens an interactive picker, which isn't suitable for an unattended, non-interactive nightly pipeline job.

choices.text: --fork-session, run once per night to create a fresh branch of the audit
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: forking a new branch each night would create a divergent session each time rather than continuing the same multi-night audit in one continuous session.

choices.text: -p alone, with no session-targeting flag, since -p guarantees the correct session is resumed automatically
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: -p controls interactive versus non-interactive execution; it doesn't provide any session-targeting guarantee on its own.

choices.text: --output-format json, since structured output guarantees session continuity across nights
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: --output-format controls response formatting, not which session is attached to — it has no bearing on session continuity.

stem: An agent needs to create a brand-new configuration file that doesn't exist yet in the repository. Which tool is appropriate?
explanation: Write handles full file replacement or new file creation — exactly the fit for creating a brand-new file that doesn't yet exist, since there's no existing content to target with a precise Edit match.

choices.text: Write
choices.reasoning: Correct: Write is documented for full file replacement or new file creation, matching exactly the case of a file that doesn't exist yet.

choices.text: Edit
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: Edit performs targeted modifications via a unique matched text within an existing file — there's no existing content to match against for a brand-new file.

choices.text: MultiEdit
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: MultiEdit performs multiple targeted edits within an existing file, which also requires existing content to match against.

choices.text: Grep
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: Grep searches file contents for a pattern — it doesn't create files.

choices.text: Glob
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: Glob finds files by path pattern — it doesn't create new files.

choices.text: Task (subagent)
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: creating a single, well-defined new file doesn't require delegating to an isolated subagent for open-ended exploration.

stem: A junior engineer proposes: "let's move our 'never push directly to main' rule from a branch-protection setting into CLAUDE.md instead, so it's easier for new hires to discover." What's the concern with this proposal?
explanation: Moving a hard, "must never happen" rule from an enforced boundary (branch protection) into CLAUDE.md would downgrade it from a structural guarantee to guidance the model may or may not follow — the opposite direction from the exam's enforcement-over-guidance principle. Discoverability for new hires is better solved by documenting the existing enforced rule in CLAUDE.md, not by replacing the enforcement itself.

choices.text: This would downgrade a structurally enforced rule to mere guidance the model may not follow; better to keep branch protection and additionally document it in CLAUDE.md for discoverability
choices.reasoning: Correct: this identifies the core concern directly — replacing an enforced boundary with CLAUDE.md guidance moves in the wrong direction, and the discoverability goal can be met by documenting the existing enforcement rather than substituting for it.

choices.text: There's no concern; CLAUDE.md and branch protection provide identical guarantees, so the swap is safe
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this directly contradicts the enforcement-versus-guidance distinction — CLAUDE.md is not an enforced boundary the way branch protection is.

choices.text: The concern is only that CLAUDE.md files load slower than branch-protection settings
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: loading performance isn't the substantive concern here; the concern is the loss of structural enforcement guarantees.

choices.text: The concern is that CLAUDE.md cannot contain any information about git workflow at all
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: CLAUDE.md can certainly document git workflow conventions as guidance — the issue is specifically about removing enforcement for a "must never happen" rule, not about topic restrictions on CLAUDE.md content.

choices.text: There's no concern, since new hires reading CLAUDE.md will always comply perfectly with the rule going forward
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this assumes perfect compliance from guidance alone, which is exactly the unreliable assumption the enforcement-over-guidance principle warns against.

choices.text: The concern is that CLAUDE.md is exclusively for personal, non-team-shared content
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: the project-level `.claude/CLAUDE.md` is explicitly team-shared and version-controlled — the actual concern here is enforcement strength, not sharing scope.

stem: During a large refactor spanning many hours, a developer wants to be able to hand off the in-progress work to a colleague who will continue it the next day, in a completely fresh session, without a lengthy verbal handoff meeting. What should the current session produce to make this possible?
explanation: A scratchpad/manifest recording key findings, the current understood data flow, open questions, risk areas, and next steps is exactly what allows a colleague starting a fresh session to pick up the work efficiently, without needing a live handoff conversation to reconstruct the same context.

choices.text: A scratchpad/manifest of key findings, current understood data flow, open questions, risk areas, and next steps, that the colleague's fresh session can read directly
choices.reasoning: Correct: this matches the documented scratchpad pattern's purpose exactly — enabling exactly this kind of asynchronous handoff between people (or sessions) without needing a live conversation to transfer context.

choices.text: Nothing structured is needed; the colleague should just start fresh and re-derive everything independently
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this discards hours of legitimate progress and understanding that the scratchpad pattern is specifically meant to preserve and hand off efficiently.

choices.text: A full raw transcript of the entire session, to be read start to finish by the colleague
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: a full raw transcript is explicitly the less efficient alternative to a structured scratchpad — the colleague would have to wade through the whole session rather than getting a targeted summary.

choices.text: Only the final git diff produced so far, with no notes on open questions or risk areas
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: a diff alone doesn't convey open questions or risk areas the colleague needs to know about to safely continue the refactor.

choices.text: A recording of the developer narrating their screen for the colleague to watch later
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this isn't structured, machine-usable state that a fresh Claude Code session could inject into its own context — the documented pattern is a written scratchpad/manifest.

choices.text: Nothing; handoffs between developers on an in-progress refactor are inherently unsupported
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: the scratchpad pattern is explicitly documented to support exactly this kind of handoff for long-running, multi-session work.
